title: Zemar Hakim
text:
Hey, glad you stopped by! I’m a PhD candidate in Economics at Queen’s University; my research focuses on identifying and understanding the social and economic causal effects of natural disasters.
I enjoy applying quantitative tools to real-world problems. In addition to my doctorate, I have worked as a consultant for the public and private sector. I spent the summer of 2026 as a Senior Associate Intern at Charles River Associates International, working in the Competition and Antitrust Practice in Toronto. Before that, I served as a Senior Research Analyst at Global Affairs Canada, where I applied data science to inform policy on Canada’s international economic security.
Use one of the links above to get in touch. Whether you’re curious about grad school, working as a professional economist, or just want to talk research, I’d love to hear from you.

Job Market Paper
Proximity to the Plague: Measuring Locust Exposure and Child Health


Abstract

Kenya’s 2019–2022 desert locust invasion offers a setting to test how the definition of “exposure” shapes both who is targeted for relief and what health effects researchers detect. Using the 2022 Demographic and Health Survey linked to georeferenced locust records, this study builds four nested exposure measures of increasing biological and agronomic rigor; locust presence, locust form, arrival during a susceptible crop stage, and NDVI-verified crop damage. The measures disagree sharply about who counts as exposed. The simple proximity measure common in the literature flags 74 percent more children than a damage-verified one at the same radius, and the additional children are disproportionately from pastoral rather than crop-dependent households, with direct implications for relief targeting. On child health, no general relationship between exposure and height, weight, or wasting outcomes is detected under looser definitions or wider radii. Under the strictest, damage-verified definition, children within 15km of a confirmed crop-damaging event show significantly lower weight-for-age and weight-for-height, an effect that decays sharply with distance and survives placebo and cluster-robustness checks. Both results — the absence of a detectable effect under common measurement choices, and its presence under a stricter one — follow directly from how exposure is defined, a choice the literature has largely treated as inconsequential.

Working Papers
Wildfire smoke, air quality, and the limits of short-run labor-market impacts in Canadian cities With Christopher S. Cotton | Submitted August 2026: Nature Climate Change


Abstract

Wildfire-smoke-driven increases in fine particulate matter raise hours worked and employment in Canada’s nine largest metropolitan areas. This response is consistent with productivity impairment requiring longer hours to meet output targets and with degraded outdoor conditions reducing the value of non-work time. Both mechanisms imply welfare losses that standard labour-market statistics record as gains, suggesting output-based damage assessments understate the costs of smoke in urban economies.

Drought-Proof Generosity: Index Insurance and Informal Livestock Lending in Northern Kenya Last updated: April, 2026


Abstract

A central concern in the microinsurance literature is whether formal insurance contracts crowd out informal risk-sharing arrangements that underpin livelihoods in developing economies. Using six rounds of panel data from pastoralist households in Marsabit, northern Kenya, we estimate the causal effect of Index-Based Livestock Insurance (IBLI) on informal livestock lending during drought. We instrument IBLI uptake with randomly distributed price discount coupons and exploit exogenous variation in drought severity measured by the Standardised Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Our two-stage least squares estimates, corrected for small-cluster bias with 16 sub-location clusters, show that IBLI coverage significantly the probability of borrowing livestock during drought—a crowding-in effect, not crowding out. A one-standard-deviation worsening of drought conditions raises the probability of livestock borrowing by roughly 39~percentage points more for insured than uninsured households. Placebo tests on livestock gifts and outward loans show no significant effects, supporting the exclusion restriction. Generalised random forest estimates reveal that treatment effect heterogeneity is driven primarily by drought severity and livestock wealth. These findings suggest that formal index insurance complements, rather than substitutes for, informal reciprocal lending networks, providing a new channel through which microinsurance improves household resilience.

title: Research

Work in Progress
Born into Drought: Early-Life Exposure and Child Health in Angola


Abstract

Observational estimates of drought’s effect on child nutrition are likely severe underestimates: treatment is measured at geographic centroids that obscure the true variation in household-level water deficit. This paper estimates the causal effect of early-life drought exposure on stunting in Angola using a shift-share instrument that interacts atmospheric circulation with cluster-level rainfall sensitivity. The 2SLS estimate implies that a one-unit deterioration in a standard moisture index during the first year of life raises stunting prevalence by 35 percentage points. The first year is the critical exposure window in this sample, dominating birth-point and second-year specifications across all instrument and treatment combinations. These findings imply that the observational literature, which reports pooled estimates corresponding to roughly 3 percentage points in stunting prevalence per unit drought, understates the true nutritional cost of early-life moisture deficit by a factor of roughly twelve, with implications for the targeting and timing of pre-emptive nutrition and water, sanitation, and hygiene interventions in drought-prone provinces of southern Africa.

title: Research
text:
Policy Papers and Other Contributions
Patent Monetization Promotion and SSO Participation With Charles River Associates


Project Details

Simcoe and Zhang (2021) study whether standard setting organizations’ intellectual property rights (IPR) policies affect participation and innovation, using two natural experiments: the W3C’s 2003 shift to royalty-free licensing and the IEEE’s 2015 revision of its patent policy. Across both settings, they find little evidence that stricter IPR terms reduced participation by standard-essential patent (SEP) licensors or innovation in patent-intensive areas, though their IEEE analysis covers only a short post-revision window. This paper extends the IEEE portion of their study — working-group contributions, organization-level contributions, and CPC-level patent applications — through 2025. The organization-level result remains a precisely estimated null over the longer window. Two other results diverge from the original findings: 802.11’s relative contribution growth becomes larger, other patent-intensive working groups now show a significant relative decline, and CPC groups more exposed to declared 802.11 patents show significantly higher post-2015 patenting. We argue these diverging results are more plausibly explained by the coincident Wi-Fi 6/6E and Wi-Fi 7 technology cycle than by the policy itself, and conclude that our extension does not overturn Simcoe and Zhang’s (2021) central finding.

G7 Sanctions Gap Analysis With Global Affairs Canada | Presented during Canada’s G7 Presidency


Project Details

This project compiled sanctions data for all five jurisdictions (US, UK, EU, Japan and Canada), recording for each affected product code and listing the specific legal citation (e.g., executive order, EU regulation article, or UK/Canada equivalent) authorizing the restriction, alongside indicators for whether the measure is an import restriction, export restriction, or listed persons. The resulting harmonized dataset allows for consistent measurement of the scope and overlap of allied sanctions regimes across countries. The report and associated analysis proivdes a foundation for measuring and understanding coordination (or divergence) toward Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the effectiveness of these measures in restricting bilateral trade flows.
